title: India's Pharma Industry Is Betting Its Future on Biosimilars — and the Numbers Suggest the Gamble May Pay Off
excerpt: With $30 billion in annual exports, the most USFDA-approved plants outside America, and a biosimilars market projected to quadruple by 2033, India's 'Pharmacy of the World' is rewriting its playbook — from cheap generics to high-value biologics.
body:
For three decades, India has worn the title "Pharmacy of the World" with a mix of pride and slight defensiveness. The pride is deserved: Indian factories churn out nearly 20 per cent of the planet's generic medicines by volume, supply 60 per cent of global vaccine demand, and operate more USFDA-approved manufacturing facilities than any country outside the United States. The defensiveness comes from knowing that most of those exports are low-margin, high-volume generic pills — the pharmaceutical equivalent of assembling someone else's design.

That story is now changing. And for NRI investors watching India's equity markets, the shift may be one of the decade's most consequential sectoral bets.

## The Numbers Behind the Pivot

India's pharmaceutical exports hit $30.47 billion in FY25, growing 9.4 per cent year-on-year, according to the Organisation of Pharmaceutical Producers of India (OPPI). But the composition of those exports is starting to look materially different.

The global biosimilars market — biological medicines that are near-identical copies of existing branded biologics, often used to treat cancer, autoimmune diseases, and chronic conditions — was valued at $28 billion in 2025. It is projected to surge to $130.1 billion by 2035, growing at a compound annual rate of 16.7 per cent, according to Roots Analysis.

India's domestic biosimilars market is on an even steeper trajectory. Valued at $1.51 billion in FY25, it is projected to reach $6.44 billion by FY33, a CAGR of nearly 20 per cent, per Markets & Data research.

"The pharmaceutical industry has the scale and capability to move up the value chain from generics to complex generics, biologics, specialty medicines and innovation-led therapies," said Parthasarathy Sampathkumar, Head of the Biocon Group Centre of Excellence, at the CPHI & PMEC India 2026 expo this week.

## What Is Driving the Shift

Several forces are converging to push Indian pharma beyond its traditional comfort zone.

**The patent cliff.** Over the next five years, biologics worth more than $200 billion in global annual sales are set to lose patent protection. These include blockbuster drugs for cancer, rheumatoid arthritis, and diabetes. For Indian companies that can develop quality biosimilar versions, the prize is enormous — margins on biosimilars typically run 40 to 70 per cent higher than on simple generics.

**Government muscle.** The Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for pharmaceuticals, the establishment of bulk drug parks, and the newly launched Biopharma SHAKTI programme are all designed to reduce India's dependence on imported active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) — many of which still come from China — while building domestic biologics capacity. Biopharma SHAKTI, in particular, is targeted at accelerating biosimilar and novel therapy development.

**Regulatory track record.** India's drug firms hold the highest number of USFDA-approved manufacturing sites outside America — a credibility asset that is hard to replicate. When the US Food and Drug Administration reached out to Indian drugmakers this month to supply the cancer drug ifosfamide during a critical shortage, it underscored a simple truth: the world trusts Indian manufacturing capacity.

**AI-driven smart manufacturing.** A growing number of Indian pharma plants are deploying artificial intelligence for quality control, yield optimisation, and drug discovery. "We will showcase our latest AI-enabled technologies designed to simplify operations, enhance productivity and deliver measurable business outcomes," said Rishal Shah, founder of serialisation technology firm Jekson Vision.

## Who Stands to Gain

The shift is not a rising tide that lifts all 3,000-plus Indian pharma companies equally. Industry watchers identify three tiers:

**Large-cap leaders** such as Biocon Biologics, Dr. Reddy's Laboratories, and Cipla are investing directly in biosimilar pipelines and global clinical trials. Biocon Biologics, backed by its acquisition of Viatris' biosimilars business, is already one of the world's largest biosimilar players by revenue.

**Mid-cap specialists** including Aurobindo Pharma, Zydus Lifesciences, and Lupin are pursuing complex generics — injectable drugs, peptides, and specialty dermatology products that command higher prices and thinner competition than oral solid dosages.

**Contract manufacturers (CDMOs and CRDMOs)** are the picks-and-shovels play. Companies like Divi's Laboratories, Syngene International, and Laurus Labs are building biologics CDMO capacity that global innovators are increasingly contracting. EY Parthenon's recent report flagged CRDMOs and Global Capability Centres (GCCs) as two of the three pillars that will define India's next pharmaceutical growth phase.

## What It Means for NRI Portfolios

For diaspora investors, the pharma pivot offers several angles.

The Nifty Pharma index gained 2.1 per cent in the trading week ended June 25 — the top-performing sector — lifted partly by the FDA's approach to Indian drugmakers for cancer drug supply and partly by the sector's relative insulation from crude oil and monsoon risks that weigh on the broader market.

More structurally, the biosimilar wave creates a multi-year earnings growth runway for the best-positioned companies. Analysts at Motilal Oswal have noted that Indian pharma's shift toward specialty and complex generics is improving the sector's margin profile even as volume growth moderates.

For NRIs working in the US and UK pharmaceutical industries, the pivot also creates a growing reverse-brain-drain pathway. Companies like Biocon, Dr. Reddy's, and Sun Pharma are actively recruiting clinical development, regulatory affairs, and biomanufacturing talent from the diaspora — roles that were scarce in India's generics-only era.

## The Risk That Cannot Be Ignored

The elephant in the room is trade policy. The United States, which accounts for 32 per cent of India's pharmaceutical exports, has reportedly considered a 200 per cent tariff on pharmaceutical imports. While generic drugs have been kept outside the tariff framework so far, the threat remains.

India's pharma exports are projected to reach $65 billion by 2030. If the tariff wall materialises, the growth trajectory would depend on how quickly Indian companies can diversify into Europe, Japan, and other regulated markets.

For now, however, the direction of travel is clear: India's pharmaceutical industry is no longer content to be the world's cheapest chemist. It wants to be the world's most capable one. The numbers — and the policy architecture — suggest it has a credible shot.
nri_angle: NRI investors and Indian-origin pharma professionals in the US and UK are watching India's shift from generics to biosimilars closely — it creates both portfolio opportunities in listed Indian pharma stocks and career pathways for reverse-brain-drain talent.
